1. FEMALES RESPOND EARLY; MALES RESPOND LATE
- Timewise-significant genes (timewise p < 0.05) per week, female: 220 -> 329 -> 501 -> 532;
  male: 145 -> 134 -> 176 -> 379. Female muscle already shows a large response at week 1 that
  grows steadily, whereas the male response stays small and flat through 4 weeks and then more
  than doubles between 4w and 8w; 251 of the 507 male-responsive genes become significant only
  at 8 weeks. 132 female genes are significant at ALL four timepoints vs only 29 male genes.
- Direction: up-regulated genes outnumber down-regulated ones at most points, increasingly so
  at 4w-8w in both sexes (female 8w: 342 up / 190 down; male 8w: 217 up / 162 down).

2. SEX DIVERGENCE EARLY, STRONG CONVERGENCE BY WEEK 8
- Female-male correlation of log fold-changes across all 766 genes rises monotonically:
  r = 0.13 (1w), 0.07 (2w), 0.43 (4w), 0.63 (8w). At 8w, 265 genes are significant in both
  sexes and 99.6% of them change in the same direction; at 1w-2w only 33-39 genes are shared
  and early regulation is largely sex-distinct (one 98-gene cluster is literally opposite in
  sign: up in females, down in males, until males flip up at 8w).
- Overall, 402 of 766 genes are responsive in both sexes, 255 are female-only and 105 male-only.

3. PREDOMINANT TEMPORAL PATTERNS (k-means on the 766-gene x 8-condition z-score matrix, k=8)
- Shared, progressive/late UP-regulation is the dominant pattern: the two largest clusters
  (n=168 and n=110, together 36% of all genes) rise in both sexes and carry the canonical
  oxidative-remodeling program - mitochondrial pyruvate carrier Mpc2, respiratory-chain and
  creatine-kinase enzymes (Cox7a2, Atp5mc1, Ckmt1, Ckmt2), GOT1/GOT2, Mt-atp6 - already visible
  from 1w-2w in females and consolidated at 4w-8w in both sexes.
- Shared DOWN-regulation (n=176): includes progressive repression of the immediate-early gene
  Fos and Prkag3 (strongest in females) and a male-specific 8-week down-shift of hexokinase Hk2,
  consistent with a late glycolytic-to-oxidative switch.
- Female-specific early pattern (n=58 + female-dominant clusters): rapid 1w-4w induction of
  lipid-mobilization genes Lipe (hormone-sensitive lipase), Fabp4 and Tbc1d1 in females but not
  males, matching the greater lipid reliance of female muscle during endurance exercise.
- Male-specific late pattern (n=63): a burst of induction at 8 weeks, including the glucose
  transporter Slc2a4 (GLUT4) - males reach the glucose-handling adaptation only at the end of
  the program.
- Sex-opposite early pattern (n=98): ECM/vascular/cytokine-receptor genes (Sox18, Il6r, Fbln1)
  up in females but down in males at 1w-2w, converging upward by 8w.

BOTTOM LINE
Both sexes converge by week 8 on the same endpoint - a broadly shared up-regulation of
mitochondrial/oxidative and glucose-handling machinery with high directional concordance
(99.6%) - but they take different temporal routes: females mount an early (1w), lipid- and
metabolism-heavy transcriptional response that is sustained throughout, while the male
transcriptome is comparatively silent until a large, concentrated response at 8 weeks. The
predominant shared pattern is progressive up-regulation of the oxidative program; the
predominant sex-specific patterns are female-early lipid-mobilization induction and a
male-late (8-week) surge.

Limitations: the table contains only pre-filtered training-regulated genes (766 in SKM-VL), so
whole-transcriptome response fractions cannot be computed; timewise significance is nominal
p < 0.05; cluster number (k=8) is an interpretability choice; and rat-to-human translation is
inferential.
da-6-2.notes: The agent correctly restricts to the TRNSCRPT × SKM-VL slice and provides strong biological interpretation and sourcing, but it does not implement the required 4-timepoint per-sex significance completeness filter or directional 4-state encoding; its sex-specific categorization and ranking are only partial.

da-6-5.answer:
DA-6-5 FINAL ANSWER
To what extent does endurance training elicit coordinated molecular responses across different organs, and which tissues exhibit the most similar changes?

EXTENT OF COORDINATION
Endurance training elicits molecular responses that are mostly tissue-specific, with a limited but detectable coordinated component that is strongly dependent on the molecular layer:

1. Feature sharing (breadth). Of 22,606 unique non-redundant training-regulated features (training_q < 0.05), 15,666 (69.3%) are regulated in exactly one tissue; only 30.7% span 2 or more tissues, 3.0% (679) span 5+, and the single broadest response (the metabolite trimethylamine-N-oxide, TMAO) reaches 16 of 20 tissues. Breadth is layer-dependent: transcripts, proteins, phosphosites, acetyl sites, methylated loci and ATAC peaks have a median breadth of 1 tissue, whereas metabolites (median 2) and immunoassay analytes (median 2.5) are shared about twice as often — the most broadly regulated features are almost all metabolites (TMAO 16, N-methylproline 14, ala-ala 13, 5-methylcytosine/ectoine 12, C3-DC carnitine 11 tissues), consistent with circulating small molecules propagating systemically.

2. Direction of change. Even when a feature is regulated in multiple tissues, the direction usually differs: only 1.4% (95/6,940) of multi-tissue features change in the same direction in every tissue where they are regulated (mean sign-concordance 0.32). Shared identity does not imply a shared response.

3. Response-profile correlation between organs. Pairwise Spearman correlations of training log fold-changes over shared features (2 sexes x 4 timepoints per feature) have median rho = 0.09 for the transcriptome (19 tissues, 145 pairs; only 15% of pairs rho > 0.3), rho = 0.37 for the metabolome (19 tissues, 158 pairs; 66% rho > 0.3) and rho = 0.47 for the proteome (7 tissues, 21 pairs; 81% rho > 0.3). Thus: strong tissue specificity at the transcript level, moderate system-wide coordination at the protein and metabolite levels (noting the proteome covers fewer tissues and metabolites are measured in many tissues by design, so cross-layer medians are not strictly comparable).

MOST SIMILAR TISSUES
- Transcriptome: the two skeletal muscles, gastrocnemius (SKM-GN) and vastus lateralis (SKM-VL), are by far the most similar pair (rho = 0.73 over 1,744 shared gene-conditions; robust in both sexes: 0.69 male / 0.78 female; highest regulated-gene-set overlap, Jaccard 0.20). Other coherent clusters match anatomical/functional relatedness: cardiovascular (HEART-VENACV rho = 0.41; HEART-SKM-GN 0.39), immune (BLOOD-SPLEEN 0.44), brain (CORTEX-HIPPOC 0.43), and gut (COLON-SMLINT). A BAT-LUNG axis is strong but female-specific (female rho = 0.68, male rho = -0.12). Central-nervous-system tissues share almost no regulated genes with peripheral organs (CORTEX Jaccard <= 0.035 with any tissue).
- Proteome: cortex-kidney (rho = 0.89), cortex-heart (0.82), cortex-lung (0.78) and kidney-lung (0.77), consistent across sexes, though cortex pairs rest on only ~50-70 shared proteins.
- Metabolome: broadly positive coordination; top pairs ovary-spleen (0.97), kidney-ovary (0.94), ovary-gastrocnemius (0.93), colon-subcutaneous adipose (0.88), cortex-hippocampus (0.79, n=96).
- Response magnitude: liver (5,951 regulated features), adrenal gland (4,605) and subcutaneous white adipose (3,115) mount the broadest responses; hypothalamus (62), vena cava (113) and testes (155) the narrowest.

TEMPORAL DYNAMICS
Coordination between related tissues strengthens with training duration rather than appearing at once: SKM-GN-SKM-VL transcriptome correlation rises monotonically from rho = 0.49 (1w) to 0.56 (2w), 0.82 (4w) and 0.89 (8w); BLOOD-SPLEEN rises from 0.24 to 0.66; the female BAT-LUNG coordination holds at rho ~ 0.51-0.59 through 4 weeks then collapses (-0.32 at 8w). Genome-wide, however, median pairwise coordination stays low (rho 0.06-0.13) at every timepoint — coordination grows for specific tissue pairs, not globally. The most broadly shared molecular response, TMAO, is uniformly down-regulated across ~16 tissues at 1-2 weeks and normalizes by 4-8 weeks, marking a systemic early metabolic phase of training.

BOTTOM LINE
Endurance training produces predominantly tissue-autonomous molecular responses (about 70% of regulated features are unique to one tissue, and even shared features usually change in different directions), superimposed with a coordinated program that (i) is strongest between anatomically/functionally related organs — the two skeletal muscles being the clearest and best-powered example, followed by heart-vena cava, blood-spleen, cortex-hippocampus and colon-small intestine; (ii) is far more pronounced in the metabolome and proteome than the transcriptome; and (iii) intensifies over the 8-week training course for muscle and immune pairs, while other axes (e.g. female BAT-lung) are transient.

Caveats: the dataset contains only significant features (truncating overlap/correlation estimates upward); assay coverage is unbalanced (proteome in 7 of 19 tissues; hypothalamus nearly unestimable); and correlations among significant features demonstrate response similarity, not shared regulatory causality.
da-6-5.notes: The agent correctly handles data loading, FDR filtering, de-duplication, and per-tissue/assay counts, but does not compute set-similarity matrices for all assays and performs no cross-assay aggregation, limiting the evaluation to per-assay interpretations rather than a single coordinated tissue-pair ranking.

da-8-1.answer:
ANSWER — DA-8-1: Hypertension-associated metabolites positively correlated with systolic blood pressure in 'Bread-spikers' (adjusted for age and BMI)

METHOD SUMMARY
- Bread-spikers: for each subject, bread meals WITHOUT a mitigator/preload (Fat/Fiber/Protein excluded) were used; per-meal rise = peak post-meal glucose minus mean pre-meal baseline (mins_since_start <= 0); rises averaged across replicates; subjects above the cohort median rise (57.61 mg/dL, n=37) = bread-spikers (n=18).
- 14 of the 18 bread-spikers had metabolomics data (38 subjects profiled; per-subject abundance = mean of replicate sample columns).
- For each of 974 metabolites: OLS regression SBP ~ log2(metabolite abundance) + age + BMI within the 14 bread-spikers; metabolites kept if coefficient > 0 and p < 0.05 (39 passed); top 10 ranked by p-value.

TOP 10 METABOLITES (beta = mmHg SBP per doubling of abundance; p from the age- and BMI-adjusted model)

1. cis-4-Hydroxyproline (feature 6.63_130.0513m/z; putative, MSI level 2; candidates include 5-aminolevulinic acid) — beta = 51.1, p = 1.1e-04
2. Proline, adduct feature (8.14_157.0968m/z) — beta = 26.3, p = 8.3e-04
3. L-Proline (8.14_115.0633n; HMDB00162 / KEGG C00148; urea cycle, arginine & proline metabolism; MSI level 1, confirmed) — beta = 29.8, p = 1.1e-03
4. Aspartyl-Arginine dipeptide (13.04_290.1453m/z; HMDB28747; putative) — beta = 18.4, p = 1.5e-03
5. Deoxycholic acid 3-glucuronide (9.52_567.3172m/z; HMDB02596 / KEGG C03033; primary bile acid metabolism; putative) — beta = 17.4, p = 1.7e-03
6. Kynurenic acid (4.28_190.0496m/z; HMDB00715 / KEGG C01717; tryptophan/kynurenine metabolism; MSI level 1, confirmed) — beta = 13.0, p = 3.2e-03
7. N-Acetylgalactosaminitol (5.88_222.0987m/z; putative) — beta = 38.5, p = 4.1e-03
8. Citrinin (4.77_250.0802n; putative) — beta = 10.7, p = 4.5e-03
9. Creatinine (0.54_114.0663m/z; HMDB00562 / KEGG C00791; creatine metabolism; MSI level 1, confirmed) — beta = 47.4, p = 7.2e-03
10. Medazepam (11.62_271.1031m/z; putative) — beta = 12.2, p = 7.8e-03

KEY POINTS
- The highest-confidence hits are L-proline (and hydroxyproline/collagen-turnover features), kynurenic acid, and creatinine — all biologically consistent with hypertension mechanisms (vascular extracellular-matrix remodeling, inflammation/endothelial dysfunction, renal function).
- Robustness: 8 of the 10 also pass p < 0.05 with positive coefficients when regressions are run on raw (untransformed) abundances.
- Caveats: n = 14 (small; nominal p<0.05, no hit survives BH-FDR across 974 tests); cross-sectional (not causal); features #1, #5, #7, #8, #10 are only putatively annotated; 4 of 18 bread-spikers lacked metabolomics data.
da-8-1.notes: Most steps are executed correctly; primary deductions due to incomplete reporting and missing R-squared.

da-8-2.answer:
INTERACTION EFFECT SIZE: Baseline insulin resistance x (protein vs fiber preload) on peak glucose reduction in rice mitigator experiments

SUMMARY ANSWER
--------------
The interaction effect size between baseline insulin-resistance (IR) status and the protein-vs-fiber difference in peak glucose reduction is -22.1 mg/dL (difference-in-differences), equivalent to a large standardized effect of about -0.89 SD (Hedges' g = -1.20; partial eta-squared = 0.070). Insulin-resistant participants show the OPPOSITE preload benefit pattern to insulin-sensitive participants: protein preloading outperforms fiber in insulin-sensitive subjects, whereas fiber outperforms protein in insulin-resistant subjects.

METHOD
------
1. From data_cgm.csv, for each subject and replicate rice trial: baseline glucose = mean of t<0 readings; peak excursion = max postprandial glucose (t 0-170 min) - baseline. Peaks were averaged across replicates per subject per arm (rice alone, rice+Protein, rice+Fiber).
2. Peak reduction = peak(rice alone) - peak(rice + mitigator). 23 subjects had all three rice arms.
3. Insulin resistance status from data_meta.csv SSPG (steady-state plasma glucose, Reaven insulin-suppression test): SSPG >= 180 mg/dL = insulin resistant. 19/23 subjects had SSPG -> 15 insulin-sensitive (IS), 4 insulin-resistant (IR).
4. Interaction = 2x2 difference-in-differences: (delta_protein - delta_fiber)_IR - (delta_protein - delta_fiber)_IS, also estimated as the IR x mitigator coefficient in an OLS model with subject-clustered standard errors.

RESULTS
-------
Mean peak-glucose reduction vs rice alone (mg/dL):
- Insulin-sensitive (n=15): protein 12.25, fiber 5.31 -> within-subject D (protein - fiber) = +6.94
- Insulin-resistant (n=4): protein 1.81, fiber 16.98 -> within-subject D = -15.17

Interaction (difference-in-differences) = (1.81 - 16.98) - (12.25 - 5.31) = -22.11 mg/dL
- OLS interaction coefficient: -22.11 +/- 13.86 (cluster-robust SE), z = -1.60, p = 0.111, 95% CI [-49.3, +5.1]
- Standardized effect: DiD / pooled SD (24.92 mg/dL) = -0.89; Hedges' g (IR vs IS on D) = -1.20; partial eta-squared = 0.070
- Welch t-test on D: t = -2.18, p = 0.086
- Robustness: median-split IR definition (SSPG >= 75) gives DiD = -12.6 mg/dL (same direction); continuous SSPG correlates negatively with D (Pearson r = -0.44, p = 0.059; Spearman r = -0.28, p = 0.244).

INTERPRETATION
--------------
The magnitude of peak glucose reduction achievable with a protein preload relative to a fiber preload decreases by ~22 mg/dL (about 0.9 SD) as baseline insulin resistance rises from sensitive to resistant. For insulin-resistant individuals, fiber preloading is the more effective peak-lowering strategy (mean 17.0 vs 1.8 mg/dL), while for insulin-sensitive individuals protein preloading is more effective (12.3 vs 5.3 mg/dL). The effect is large but imprecisely estimated (only 4 insulin-resistant participants; p = 0.11), so it should be treated as a strong but not formally significant effect-modification signal. See trace.md for full details and references.
da-8-2.notes: The agent performed the peak glucose calculations correctly but misclassified insulin resistance using SSPG cutoff instead of DI/median split, which cascaded into incorrect group sizes and interaction statistics. The interaction model was not a standard two-way ANOVA and effect size categorization was incomplete.

da-8-3.answer:
TASK DA-8-3 — FINAL ANSWER

Setup: The spiker labels are not stored in any file, so they were reconstructed from the CGM data (data_cgm.csv, plain-food challenges only). For each subject and food, the baseline-subtracted peak glucose excursion was computed (mean of pre-meal readings subtracted from the maximum post-meal value, replicates averaged). Of 38 CGM subjects, 36 had both Potato and Grape curves: 15 were classified as potato-spikers (potato peak > grape peak; XB1, XB2, XB21, XB33, XB38, XB42, XB43, XB48, XB68, XB70, XB89, XB94, XB100, XB111, XB115) and 21 as grape-spikers. Differential abundance (Welch t-test on subject-level log2 abundances, metabolomics + targeted lipidomics matrices combined; 26 of the 36 subjects have omics data) was used to rank 1,354 features.

TOP 10 DIFFERENTIALLY ABUNDANT METABOLITES (potato-spikers vs grape-spikers, ranked by p-value):
 1. FFA(16:0) palmitic acid        — up in potato-spikers (log2FC +0.17, FC 1.12, p=1.9e-4)
 2. FFA(18:1) oleic acid           — up in potato-spikers (log2FC +0.40, FC 1.32, p=5.1e-4)
 3. FFA(22:1) erucic acid          — up in potato-spikers (log2FC +0.16, FC 1.12, p=7.7e-4)
 4. Butein (chalconoid)            — down in potato-spikers (log2FC -0.17, FC 0.89, p=7.7e-4)
 5. Parabanic acid                 — up in potato-spikers (log2FC +0.34, FC 1.27, p=1.2e-3)
 6. 4-Hydroxybutyric acid (GHB)    — up in potato-spikers (log2FC +0.47, FC 1.38, p=1.3e-3)
 7. Acrylfentanyl (xenobiotic ID)  — down in potato-spikers (log2FC -0.48, FC 0.72, p=1.7e-3)
 8. FFA(17:0) margaric acid        — up in potato-spikers (log2FC +0.16, FC 1.12, p=1.9e-3)
 9. Tauroursodeoxycholic acid      — up in potato-spikers (log2FC +2.01, FC 4.04, p=1.9e-3)
10. FFA(20:2) eicosadienoic acid   — up in potato-spikers (log2FC +0.25, FC 1.19, p=2.6e-3)

The dominant biological signal is a coordinated elevation of circulating free fatty acids in potato-spikers, independently confirmed by the clinical free-fatty-acid assay in the metadata (0.47 vs 0.16 mmol/L in the 18 measured participants). Potato-spikers are also markedly more insulin-resistant and beta-cell-impaired than grape-spikers: SSPG 183.6 vs 75.3 mg/dL (p=1.0e-4), HOMA-IR 2.80 vs 1.62 (p=0.033), Disposition Index 1.24 vs 2.36 (p=0.0076), HbA1c 5.75% vs 5.42% (p=0.027).

LIPID SPECIES AMONG THE TOP 10 AND MEDIATION:
Five of the top 10 are lipid species, all free fatty acids: FFA(16:0), FFA(18:1), FFA(22:1), FFA(17:0), FFA(20:2). For each, a formal mediation analysis (group -> lipid -> outcome; Baron-Kenny paths, Sobel test, verified by 5,000-sample bootstrap) was run against two insulin-resistance outcomes (SSPG, HOMA-IR) and two beta-cell-function outcomes (Disposition Index, HOMA-B), n = 23-26 subjects.

RESULT: None of the five lipid species shows a statistically significant mediating effect for any outcome — all Sobel p-values >= 0.20 and all bootstrap 95% confidence intervals for the indirect effect include zero. The group -> lipid paths are all highly significant (p < 0.003), but the lipid -> outcome paths (adjusted for group) are not.

The strongest, directionally consistent (but non-significant) mediator candidates are for insulin resistance measured by SSPG, where elevated FFAs in potato-spikers partially account for their higher SSPG:
  - FFA(16:0) palmitic acid: indirect effect +31.2 mg/dL, Sobel z = 1.24, p = 0.216 (~27% of the total group effect; total effect on SSPG attenuates from 114.3 to 83.1 mg/dL when FFA(16:0) is included)
  - FFA(22:1) erucic acid: indirect +30.2 mg/dL, z = 1.27, p = 0.204
  - FFA(20:2) eicosadienoic acid: indirect +20.1 mg/dL, z = 1.12, p = 0.263
For HOMA-IR, HOMA-B and the Disposition Index, indirect effects are smaller and inconsistent in sign (all p > 0.3).

INTERPRETATION: The trends are mechanistically plausible — chronically elevated FFAs (especially palmitate) drive peripheral insulin resistance via the Randle cycle and DAG/PKCtheta interference with insulin signaling, which would raise SSPG — but with only 23-26 subjects the mediation analysis is underpowered and cannot confirm any lipid species as a statistically significant mediator. CONCLUSION: among the top 10 differentially abundant metabolites, the lipid species are FFA(16:0), FFA(18:1), FFA(22:1), FFA(17:0) and FFA(20:2); none of them statistically mediates the group differences in insulin resistance (SSPG/HOMA-IR) or beta-cell function (DI/HOMA-B) at p < 0.05, although FFA(16:0), FFA(22:1) and FFA(20:2) show the largest, non-significant partial-mediation trends for SSPG.

Caveats: the spiker classification was reconstructed from CGM peaks (an iAUC-based rule reassigns 12/36 subjects); no top-10 feature survives Benjamini-Hochberg FDR (min q ~ 0.25); some xenobiotic annotations (e.g. "Acrylfentanyl") are likely annotation artifacts; and cross-sectional abundances cannot establish causal mediation.
da-8-3.notes: The agent performed robust differential abundance and lipid identification but deviated from the rubric by using a cross-food spiker classification rather than per-food median splits, completely omitting phenotype correlation analyses, and failing to satisfy the mediation criteria.

da-9-1.answer:
BASELINE CIRCULATING T CELL BIOMARKERS FOR 1-YEAR OVERALL SURVIVAL UNDER PD-1 BLOCKADE
PRINCE trial (PICI0002), Arm A1: gemcitabine/nab-paclitaxel + nivolumab (nivo/chemo), n=34

METHODS SUMMARY
Baseline (C1D1, pre-treatment) CyTOF frequencies of 13 circulating cell populations were tested for
association with 1-year overall survival (dead <=365 d vs alive >=365 d; 4 patients censored before
day 365 excluded from the binary endpoint). 25 of 34 A1 patients had baseline CyTOF; the binary
analysis used 21 patients (13 alive at 1 y, 8 dead by 1 y). Populations were screened with two-sided
Mann-Whitney U tests (Benjamini-Hochberg FDR) and confirmed with univariable Cox proportional-hazards
models and median-split Kaplan-Meier/log-rank analysis on all 25 patients using full follow-up.

ANSWER — four baseline circulating T cell populations emerged as candidate associative biomarkers:

1. Ki-67+ T cells (% of CD3+ cells) — ADVERSE biomarker.
   Lower baseline frequency in 1-year survivors (median 0.933 vs 0.983 of CD3+ cells).
   Mann-Whitney p = 0.0034 (BH-FDR = 0.030), AUC = 0.125.
   Cox HR per SD = 2.28 (95% CI 1.04-4.98, p = 0.040).
   Median split: 1-year OS 33% (high) vs 100% (low), log-rank p = 0.010.
   Interpretation: high baseline proliferation of circulating T cells marks systemic inflammation /
   tumor-driven lymphocyte turnover associated with aggressive disease that chemo + anti-PD-1 cannot
   overcome.

2. NKT cells (% of leukocytes) — FAVORABLE biomarker (largest effect).
   ~4x higher in survivors (median 0.0198 vs 0.0049 of leukocytes).
   Mann-Whitney p = 0.0045 (BH-FDR = 0.030), AUC = 0.865.
   Cox HR per SD = 0.39 (0.17-0.91, p = 0.029).
   Median split: 1-year OS 90% (high) vs 36% (low), log-rank p = 0.0049.
   Interpretation: NKT cells bridge innate and adaptive immunity and license DC/CD8 responses,
   plausibly supporting benefit from PD-1 blockade.

3. Tbet+ TCRgd+ T cells (% of TCRgd T cells) — FAVORABLE biomarker (strongest continuous signal).
   Mann-Whitney p = 0.030, AUC = 0.788.
   Cox HR per SD = 0.30 (0.15-0.60, p = 0.0007).
   Median split: 1-year OS 81% (high) vs 45% (low), log-rank p = 0.025.
   Interpretation: Tbet marks type-1/cytotoxic polarization; Tbet+ gamma-delta T cells are
   IFN-gamma-producing antitumor effectors.

4. Tbet+ T cells (% of CD3+ cells) — FAVORABLE biomarker (weaker).
   Mann-Whitney p = 0.064, AUC = 0.750; Cox HR per SD = 0.52 (0.25-1.09, p = 0.085).
   Median split: 1-year OS 81% (high) vs 45% (low), log-rank p = 0.011.
   Interpretation: a pre-existing Th1/type-1-polarized circulating T cell compartment favors durable
   benefit from PD-1 blockade.

NOT ASSOCIATED: bulk/lineage T cell measures — HLA-DR+ T cells (p = 0.92), HLA-DR+ non-naive CD4
(p = 0.92), HLA-DR+ non-naive CD8 (p = 0.86) — nor non-T-cell populations (m-MDSC p = 0.80, B cells
p = 0.21, pDC p = 0.91). One discordant non-T-cell signal: CD1C+ CD141+ DC adverse in Cox (HR 1.88,
p = 0.014) but null for the 1-year binary endpoint (p = 0.35).

KEY CAVEATS
- The four T cell signals are strongly inter-correlated (|r| = 0.53-0.93): Ki-67+ T cells anticorrelates
  with NKT (r = -0.93) and Tbet+ T cells (r = -0.89). They read out one coherent "baseline T cell
  activation state" axis (high Ki-67 / low NKT / low Tbet -> poor 1-year outcome), not four independent
  biomarkers.
- Signals are not explained by Age or ECOG performance status (markers uncorrelated with ECOG,
  all p >= 0.24; age balanced between outcome groups, p = 0.35).
- Very small cohort (n = 21-25), 26% of A1 patients lack baseline CyTOF, only Ki-67+ T cells and NKT
  cells pass FDR < 0.05 in the binary screen. Findings are hypothesis-generating and associative;
  single-arm data cannot separate prognostic from treatment-predictive value, and no independent
  validation cohort exists.

BOTTOM LINE
Among nivo/chemo-treated metastatic pancreatic cancer patients, baseline circulating Ki-67+ T cells
(high = adverse), NKT cells (high = favorable), and Tbet+ (especially TCR-gamma-delta+) T cells
(high = favorable) are the circulating T cell populations most strongly associated with 1-year overall
survival, together forming a baseline T cell proliferation/type-1-polarization signature.
da-9-1.notes: The agent performed comprehensive analyses and correctly identified the main T-cell signals, but deviations in cohort filtering, feature selection, and reporting accuracy prevent full marks on several criteria.

da-9-7.answer:
PRINCE trial (PICI0002), DA-9-7: Do circulating immune-cell frequencies correlate with serum protein levels on-treatment at C2D1?

ANSWER: No — there are no statistically significant correlations between circulating immune-cell frequencies (CyTOF) and serum protein levels (Olink) at C2D1 in this dataset.

ANALYSIS: 73 of 108 randomized PRINCE patients had matched C2D1 CyTOF cell-population frequencies and C2D1 Olink proteomics; 65 had complete data (arm A1 nivo+chemo n=23, arm B2 sotigalimab+chemo n=21, arm C2 combination n=21). At C2D1, the curated CyTOF file contains only 4 cell populations (CCR7+ CD11b+ CD27- B cells, Conventional DC, HLA-DR+ Non-Naive CD4 T cells, HLA-DR+ Non-Naive CD8 T cells), and the Olink file contains 30 proteins (IFN-g, CXCL9, CXCL10, IL-2, IL-6, IL-8, IL-10, soluble PD-1, ARG1, VEGF A, etc.). All 4 x 30 = 120 pairs were tested with Spearman rank correlation (frequencies log10-transformed for the Pearson sensitivity check; Olink NPX already on a log2 scale).

RESULTS:
- Pooled (n=65): 0/120 pairs significant at nominal p<0.05 (max |rho| = 0.233, B cells vs CXCL9, p=0.062); 0/120 after Benjamini-Hochberg FDR (min q=0.31) or Bonferroni. Pearson sensitivity: 1/120 nominal (p=0.034), 0/120 after FDR.
- Arm-stratified: no significant pairs in arms A1 or B2. In arm C2 (combination, n=21), HLA-DR+ Non-Naive CD4 T-cell frequency correlated negatively with IFN-g (rho=-0.588, p=0.005), CXCL9 (rho=-0.460, p=0.036) and CXCL10 (rho=-0.442, p=0.045) at the nominal level only; none survived within-arm FDR (min q=0.08) — hypothesis-generating at best.

CONCLUSION: At the C2D1 on-treatment timepoint, frequencies of the measured circulating immune-cell populations and serum levels of the 30 measured proteins vary independently across PRINCE patients. Neither cellular frequencies nor serum proteins can serve as surrogates for one another in biomarker validation at this timepoint. The analysis is powered to detect only moderate-to-strong correlations (|rho| >= ~0.34 at n=65; |rho| >= ~0.58 per arm), is restricted to the 4 cell populations actually measured at C2D1 in this curated dataset, and is cross-sectional (baseline-to-C2D1 changes might show coupling even though C2D1 levels do not).

Outputs: trace.md (full analysis), correlation_results_pooled.csv, correlation_results_by_arm.csv, c2d1_cytof_olink_correlations.png.
da-9-7.notes: The agent performs substantial correct data harmonisation and Spearman correlation with appropriate stratification, but it deviates from the required feature scope (using 4×30=120 instead of 3×4=12 pairs), which leads to over-conservative FDR correction and the missed expected Arm C2 FDR-significant finding.

da-10-1.answer:
DA-10-1: ML Screening of Membraneless Organelle Participants — Final Answer
===========================================================================

DATA
----
sequence_prediction_filtered.xlsx: 48,504 proteins x 23 columns. Labels: SaPS=128 (PS-Self),
PdPS=214 (PS-Part), NoPS=48,158; human subsets hSaPS=59, hPdPS=96, hNoPS=8,801 (all human-only,
mutually exclusive). Scores available: PScore, PLAAC, catGRANULE (plus *_rnk percentiles and
SaPS/PdPS 8/10-feature ML classifiers). FuzDrop scores are NOT present in the data.
idr_ranges.xlsx: 55,056 IDR intervals (UniProt, start, end).

1. AMINO-ACID COMPOSITION: PS-SELF (SaPS) vs PS-PART (PdPS)
-----------------------------------------------------------
Full-sequence per-AA Mann-Whitney tests (BH FDR, 20 tests): 13/20 residues differ significantly.
- SaPS is enriched (delta freq, Cliff's delta) in G (+2.9 pp, d=+0.40), P (+1.3, +0.21),
  S (+1.0, +0.18), Q (+0.8, +0.20), T (+0.7); depleted in L (-1.6, -0.36), K (-1.3, -0.28),
  E (-1.1, -0.27), I (-0.9, -0.30), R (-0.8), D (-0.7), V (-0.5), H (-0.3), C (-0.3).
  => PS-Self proteins carry a low-complexity, polar/glycine-rich self-assembly signature;
     PS-Part proteins are more hydrophobic- and charged-residue rich, closer to a generic
     disordered interactome.
- The same pattern holds within the human subsets (hSaPS vs hPdPS: G +2.6 pp, L -1.6, K -1.4,
  E -1.4; all q<0.05), so it is not a species-mixture artifact.
- Disorder: median IDR fraction SaPS 0.282 > PdPS 0.166 >> NoPS 0.012 (MWU p=3.1e-5, 5.8e-34,
  3.4e-23). IDR-restricted (pooled) composition: SaPS IDRs enriched in G, Q, F, N, Y
  (aromatic/polar "stickers") and depleted in K, R, E, S, A vs PdPS IDRs (chi-square, q<0.05) —
  SaPS IDRs favor aromatic/polar sticker-driven self-interaction; PdPS IDRs are charge-rich,
  consistent with partner (e.g. RNA/scaffold) dependence.
- Both PS classes differ strongly from NoPS (16/20 and 14/20 residues significant; NoPS is
  structured-protein-like: Leu 9.9%, Cys 2.0%, Trp 1.2%).

2. PREDICTOR PERFORMANCE (AUROC [95% bootstrap CI]; AUPRC; base rate)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Benchmark            PScore              PLAAC               catGRANULE          FuzDrop
SaPS vs NoPS         0.831 [.791-.869]   0.834 [.794-.874]   0.817 [.777-.854]   n/a (no scores)
                     AUPRC 0.050         AUPRC 0.028         AUPRC 0.035         (base 0.0026)
PdPS vs NoPS         0.662 [.624-.699]   0.644 [.603-.684]   0.706 [.673-.741]   n/a
                     AUPRC 0.012         AUPRC 0.011         AUPRC 0.012         (base 0.0044)
hSaPS vs hNoPS       0.813 [.754-.870]   0.831 [.766-.892]   0.813 [.757-.864]   n/a
                     AUPRC 0.133         AUPRC 0.120         AUPRC 0.062         (base 0.0067)
hPdPS vs hNoPS       0.689 [.635-.742]   0.640 [.575-.702]   0.726 [.677-.774]   n/a
                     AUPRC 0.030         AUPRC 0.029         AUPRC 0.029         (base 0.0108)
All 12 Mann-Whitney tests significant (p <= 2.3e-10).

Key findings:
- All three available predictors separate PS-Self from non-PS well (AUROC ~0.81-0.83 in both
  species-wide and human benchmarks; CIs overlapping -> the three are statistically tied for SaPS).
- All predictors are much weaker for PS-Part (AUROC 0.64-0.73): partner-dependent phase separation
  is only modestly predictable from the unmodified protein sequence.
- For PdPS the ranking is consistent in both panels: catGRANULE (0.706/0.726) > PScore
  (0.662/0.689) > PLAAC (0.644/0.640) — catGRANULE's inclusion of RNA-binding/disorder terms
  likely explains its edge for partner-dependent (often RNA-dependent) condensate proteins.
- Predictors correlate only moderately (Spearman 0.42-0.60), capturing partly orthogonal features.

Threshold analysis on the human proteome (hSaPS/hPdPS vs 8,801 hNoPS; published cutoffs):
- PScore>4:  precision 6.2%/4.7%, recall 40.7%/19.6%, FPR 4.5% (Fisher p 5.3e-17 / 2.1e-7)
- PLAAC>0:   precision 5.1%/3.6%, recall 59.3%/25.0%, FPR 7.4% (p 2.4e-24 / 1.3e-7)
- catGRANULE>0: precision 1.0%/1.5%, recall 96.6%/87.5%, FPR 61.5% (p 3.6e-10 / 3.2e-8)
=> PScore and PLAAC are specific but miss most PdPS proteins; catGRANULE at score 0 is very
   sensitive but permissive (61.5% of non-PS proteome scores positive). Precision at fixed
   cutoffs is inherently low because PS classes are rare (0.7-1.1% prevalence).

3. FuzDrop
----------
FuzDrop scores are absent from the provided table, and the public server (fuzdrop.bio.unipd.it)
is a client-side web app with no bulk/API route, so FuzDrop could not be benchmarked quantitatively
here. By design (Hardenberg et al. 2020, PNAS 117:33254-62; Hatos et al. 2022, NAR 50:W337-44)
it predicts per-residue droplet-promoting regions and the probability p_D of SPONTANEOUS LLPS,
so it is expected to rank with PScore for self-assembling (SaPS) proteins but to be comparatively
weak for partner-dependent (PdPS) proteins whose condensation requires RNA or partner scaffolds.

BOTTOM LINE
-----------
PS-Self proteins have a distinctive sequence signature (G/P/S/Q-rich, aromatic/polar-sticker-rich
IDRs, highly disordered) that PScore, PLAAC and catGRANULE all capture (AUROC ~0.82-0.83). PS-Part
proteins are compositionally much closer to the ordinary proteome (charge/hydrophobic-rich IDRs,
less disorder) and are only weakly discriminated by all sequence-based predictors (AUROC 0.64-0.73),
with catGRANULE performing best. This supports a model in which partner-dependent phase separation
relies on multivalency supplied by binding partners (e.g. RNA) rather than on intrinsic sequence
propensity, and motivates combined/partner-aware predictors for MLO participant screening.

LIMITATIONS
-----------
FuzDrop unevaluated (no scores); NoPS = proteome background, not experimentally validated negatives;
small positive sets (59-214) give wide CIs; IDR intervals lack organism/isoform metadata; low
precision at published thresholds reflects class rarity, not only predictor error.
da-10-1.notes: The work is strong overall but has notable gaps in frequency normalization (per-protein vs pooled), missing fold-change computation, and incomplete use of property/IDR-based ordering; predictor AUC evaluation and summarization are excellent.

da-10-3.answer:
FINAL ANSWER — DA-10-3: Do phase-separation predictors perform consistently better on MLO participant datasets than on membrane-bound organelle controls?

ANSWER: YES — with an important qualifier. The machine-learning phase-separation classifiers (PdPS-10fea, SaPS-10fea, PdPS-8fea, SaPS-8fea) and catGRANULE consistently and strongly discriminate members of all four membraneless-organelle (MLO) participant datasets from the fixed hNoPS background, while showing little or no enrichment on the membrane-bound/aggregate control datasets. In contrast, the physicochemical predictors PScore and PLAAC (and the sparsely available DeepPhase) fail as MLO screens on both dataset classes, so the "consistently better on MLO" conclusion holds for the ML-based predictors but not for the simple physicochemical scores.

METHOD IN BRIEF
- Analysis universe: the 20,375 Homo sapiens rows of sequence_prediction.xlsx (all six SaPS/PdPS scores + catGRANULE complete), joined to the hSaPS/hPdPS/hNoPS flags (h_combined_with_flags.xlsx; 8,799 hNoPS proteins in-universe) and to the six 0/1 dataset flags from List_of_proteins_for_comparing_MLO_enrichment.xlsx.
- Primary evaluation sheet: "Training proteins removed" (3,813 entries) — verified to exclude all 59 hSaPS and 96 hPdPS training proteins (0 residual overlap in every dataset flag), so the SaPS/PdPS scores are evaluated without training-set leakage.
- Metric: AUROC of each predictor for dataset members (flag=1) vs the hNoPS background (n≈8,300–8,800 negatives per cell), with one-sided Mann–Whitney U p-values; MLO sets = OpenCell nuclear punctae (n=115), DACT1-particulate proteome (251), G3BP1 proximity labeling (241), PhaSepDB high-throughput (1,712); controls = mitochondrial proteomics (1,120, membrane-bound organelle) and amyloid fiber-forming proteins (62, solid aggregates).

KEY RESULTS (AUROC vs hNoPS, training-removed sheet)

1. ML classifiers are strongly enriched on every MLO dataset:
   - PdPS-10fea: 0.76 (OpenCell) / 0.83 (DACT1) / 0.84 (G3BP1) / 0.77 (PhaSepDB); mean 0.800.
   - SaPS-10fea: 0.67 / 0.78 / 0.82 / 0.69; mean 0.739.
   - PdPS-8fea: mean 0.670; SaPS-8fea: mean 0.644; catGRANULE: mean 0.644.
   All 20 ML-classifier × MLO-dataset cells are significant (Mann–Whitney p from 2e-8 down to 1e-268).

2. The same predictors drop to near-chance on membrane-bound controls:
   - Mitochondrial proteome: SaPS-8fea 0.465 (p≈1.0), PdPS-8fea 0.472 (p≈1.0), SaPS-10fea 0.489, PdPS-10fea 0.562, catGRANULE 0.522 — i.e. essentially no MLO-type signal in a membrane-bound organelle.
   - Amyloid fiber-forming proteins: slightly above chance for the 10-feature classifiers (PdPS-10fea 0.602, p=0.003; SaPS-10fea 0.573, p=0.024), consistent with shared aggregation-prone sequence features, but far below MLO values; the 8-feature classifiers are at chance (0.507/0.461).

3. Formal "consistently better" test: mean MLO AUROC minus mean control AUROC is positive for all 7 predictors (PdPS-10fea +0.218, SaPS-10fea +0.208, PdPS-8fea +0.181, SaPS-8fea +0.181, catGRANULE +0.148, PScore +0.029, PLAAC +0.027); one-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank across predictors: p = 0.0078 (the minimum possible with n=7). 25 of 28 predictor × MLO-dataset AUROCs exceed the best control AUROC of the same predictor (the 3 exceptions are PScore/PLAAC cells that discriminate nothing).

4. PScore and PLAAC do NOT screen MLOs: PScore AUROC 0.40–0.52 on MLO datasets (e.g. 0.404 on DACT1, p≈1.0; 0.522 on OpenCell, p=0.22); PLAAC 0.34–0.50 (anti-correlated on DACT1, 0.336). Their MLO-vs-control differences (+0.03) are negligible. DeepPhase (available for only 5,333 proteins, 0 PhaSepDB coverage) was likewise inconsistent (0.39–0.59).

5. Screening view: at a threshold admitting 10% of the hNoPS background, PdPS-10fea recovers 38–51% of each MLO dataset (mean 44%) vs 10.6% of the mitochondrial proteome and 21% of amyloid formers; SaPS-10fea recovers 32–40% (mean 35%) vs 6.8%/19%. SaPS-8fea: 22% vs 3.6%/9.7%.

6. PdPS > SaPS on every MLO dataset (e.g. DACT1: 0.832 vs 0.775), consistent with the scaffold/client model: most proteome-scale MLO participants are recruited partner (client) proteins, not self-assembling scaffolds.

7. Robustness: repeating on the "Original data" sheet (training proteins included) inflates AUROCs by 0.001–0.054 without changing any ranking — confirming leakage control matters and the reported numbers are conservative. Using "all non-member proteins" instead of hNoPS as negatives leaves the MLO-minus-control gap intact (e.g. PdPS-10fea 0.766 vs 0.542).

CONCLUSION
PS predictors do perform consistently better on MLO participant datasets than on membrane-bound organelle controls, but the effect is carried by the machine-learning classifiers — especially the 10-feature PdPS and SaPS models (mean MLO AUROC 0.74–0.80 vs 0.53–0.58 on controls, a +0.21 AUROC gap) — and, to a lesser degree, catGRANULE (+0.15). PScore and PLAAC provide essentially no MLO screening power. The mitochondrial control demonstrates that the enrichment is specific to condensate biology rather than generic proteomic detectability, and the weak amyloid signal indicates the 10-feature models partially capture solid-aggregation propensity in addition to liquid–liquid phase separation.

LIMITATIONS
The hNoPS background is defined by absence from the SaPS/PdPS positive sets rather than by experimental non-PS validation; only two control datasets (mitochondria, amyloid) were available; the four MLO datasets are biologically overlapping, so per-dataset AUROCs are not fully independent (mitigated by the predictor-level paired test); and PdPS/SaPS models were trained on interaction/colocalization-type data related in kind to some evaluation sets, although the training-removed sheet eliminates direct protein-level leakage.
da-10-3.notes: The agent's work is thorough and rigorous across most criteria, with only a minor omission in explicitly checking and documenting overlap removal between positive dataset members and the fixed hNoPS background, leading to a B for label construction rather than A.

da-11-1.answer:
FINAL ANSWER — DA-11-1: Ligand–receptor communication between KIR+CD8+ T cells and pathogenic CD4+ T cells in celiac disease (GSE193442)

ANALYSIS SUMMARY
All 10 samples (6 active CeD, 4 HC; 72,177 cells, 33,562 genes) were QC-filtered to 69,623 cells, normalized (CP10k + log1p), embedded by TruncatedSVD-PCA and clustered with a 30-NN Jaccard-Louvain pipeline (59 clusters). Marker annotation identified:
- KIR+CD8+ T cells = cluster 12 (n=1,313): CD8A/B+, GNLY/GZMB/GZMH/PRF1-high, TBX21+, ZNF683(Hobit)+, KLRD1+; 56.5% of CeD cells in this cluster express KIR (KIR3DL1/KIR2DL3) vs 34.2% in HC. Sender pool for communication analysis: 436 KIR+CD8 cells from CeD.
- Pathogenic CD4 proxy = cytotoxic CD4+CD8- cells expressing GNLY/PRF1/GZMB/GZMH or NKG7+KLRG1+ (gliadin-specific CD4 T cells in CeD acquire this cytotoxic phenotype; TCR data unavailable). Receiver pool: 931 CeD cells.
A CellPhoneDB/CellChat-style analysis (69 curated LR pairs, complex-min rule, score = mean(ligand)xmean(receptor), 1,000 label permutations, BH-FDR) was run sender=KIR+CD8 -> receiver=pathogenic CD4.

TOP SIGNALING PATHWAYS BEYOND MHC-I (ranked by pathway score / permutation significance):

1. GALECTIN pathway — LGALS1 -> CD69 (top pair: score 1.32, perm p=0.001, padj=0.003). Galectin-1 is expressed by 78% of KIR+CD8 cells and is strongly CeD-induced (padj=1e-23); CD69 is on 47% of pathogenic CD4 cells. Galectin-1 triggers apoptosis and Th1 suppression of activated T cells — the leading candidate for the direct non-MHC-I suppressive arm.

2. CYTOTOXIC-EFFECTOR delivery — GNLY -> PGRMC1 and GZMB -> PGRMC1 (scores 0.32/0.20, padj=0.003). Granulysin (89% of senders) and granzyme B (93% of senders; CeD-upregulated, padj=2e-04) mediate the cytotoxic killing of the targeted CD4 cells seen in vitro.

3. CCL CHEMOKINE recruitment — CCL5 -> CCR4/CCR5, CCL4 -> CCR5, CCL3 -> CCR5 (pathway total 0.449; CCL5 in 100% and CCL4 in 77% of KIR+CD8 cells; all padj=0.003). Recruits/positions pathogenic CD4 cells for contact-dependent suppression.

4. TNF SUPERFAMILY — TNFSF14 (LIGHT) -> TNFRSF14 (HVEM) (score 0.089, padj=0.003). LIGHT is CeD-induced in KIR+CD8 cells (padj=0.015) and HVEM is on 45% of pathogenic CD4 cells; LIGHT-HVEM delivers apoptosis/anti-proliferative signals to activated T cells.

5. DEATH RECEPTOR — FASLG -> FAS (score 0.016, padj=0.003). FASLG is upregulated in CeD KIR+CD8 cells and is a specific feature of the KIR+ population vs other CD8 cells (padj=1e-06); FAS on 12% of pathogenic CD4 cells enables activation-induced cell death.

6. TGF-beta — TGFB1 -> TGFBR1/TGFBR2 (TGFB1 in 55% of senders, KIR+CD8-specific vs other CD8, padj=1e-19; TGFBR2 on 28% of receivers). Soluble immunosuppression of the pathogenic CD4 compartment.

7. ADHESION/CO-RECEPTOR stabilization — CD58 -> CD2 (padj=0.003) stabilizes the effector:target conjugate for granule delivery. CD48 -> CD2 and ICAM3 -> LFA-1 score highly but are NOT population-specific (permutation n.s.) and are best viewed as generic T-cell adhesion.

Benchmark: the established MHC-I -> KIR axis (HLA-A/B/C -> KIR2DL3/3DL1, HLA-E -> KLRC1/KLRD1) aggregated score 0.236 — below the Galectin, SLAM and CCL pathway totals — confirming that pathways beyond MHC-I dominate the predicted suppressive/cytotoxic network.

INTERPRETATION: The data support a multi-layered mechanism in which CeD-expanded KIR+CD8+ T cells (i) home to and conjugate with activated pathogenic CD4 T cells via CCL chemokines and CD58/CD2 adhesion, (ii) suppress them through galectin-1-CD69, LIGHT-HVEM and TGF-beta signaling, and (iii) eliminate them through granulysin/granzyme-B and FASLG-FAS cytotoxicity — complementing the established MHC-I/KIR recognition.

LIMITATIONS: Transcript-level LR inference does not prove protein-level or functional interaction; gliadin specificity is inferred from the cytotoxic CD4 phenotype (no TCR/tetramer data); dropout deflates low-expression checkpoint receptors (PDCD1/CTLA4/TIGIT scored low); single-cell permutation significance is optimistic relative to the 6-vs-4 sample-level statistics; the curated 69-pair LR list is not exhaustive.
da-11-1.notes: The agent performed a thorough analysis with strong QC, clustering, and pathway-level interpretation, but missed UMAP/t-SNE visualization, lacked a dedicated activated CD4 marker set, used fixed thresholds for cell identification, and only computed one-directional LR scoring, leading to minor deductions.

da-12-2.answer:
Yes. The G2M checkpoint (MSigDB HALLMARK_G2M_CHECKPOINT) is significantly enriched at p < 0.05 among the DEGs shared between the overexpression (A549) and knockdown (H1299) in-vitro experiments.

Analysis: The two DEG lists in TS7.xlsx (3,260 overexpression DEGs; 5,314 knockdown DEG records, 5,290 unique genes) share 1,543 genes, as marked by the "v" overlap flags in both directions (the two flagged sets are identical; a raw name intersection gives 1,545, differing only by two unflagged genes, AC126755.1 and AC138969.2). Testing over-representation of the 200-gene G2M checkpoint set among these 1,543 shared DEGs against the background of all 7,005 DEGs detected in either experiment (121 G2M genes present in background) gives a 2x2 table of [[37, 1506], [84, 5378]]: 37 of 1,543 shared DEGs (2.40%) are G2M checkpoint genes versus 84 of 5,462 non-shared DEGs (1.54%). A one-sided Fisher's exact test (equivalent to a hypergeometric test) yields odds ratio = 1.57, p = 0.0171 < 0.05. The G2M checkpoint ranks 3rd among all 50 Hallmark sets by nominal p-value (behind HALLMARK_MITOTIC_SPINDLE, p = 2.9e-08, and HALLMARK_UV_RESPONSE_DN, p = 1.9e-04), though it does not survive Benjamini-Hochberg correction across all 50 sets (FDR = 0.286).

The 37 shared G2M checkpoint genes include canonical G2/M and mitotic regulators such as TOP2A, PLK4, KIF20B, KNL1, INCENP, ESPL1, SMC1A, SMC4, RAD21, NUMA1, LMNB1, BRCA2, POLE, WRN, XPO1 and HIF1A, indicating that the manipulated noncoding RNA(s) reproducibly affect a mitotic cell-cycle transcriptional program in lung adenocarcinoma cells. Caveat: the result is significant at the nominal p < 0.05 threshold asked in the question, but not after multiple-testing correction across all Hallmark pathways.
da-12-2.notes: Agent performs correct gene list extraction and ORA with clear methods, but uses a conservative DEG-union background yielding p/FDR values that differ from rubric expected values, and global pathway reporting is partially incomplete.

da-12-4.answer:
No — Kocuria is NOT significantly associated with poor prognosis in lung cancer patients with matched tumor-sample microbiome and RNA-seq data.

Analysis: Univariate Cox Proportional Hazards models were fit for each of the 250 microbial genera in the matched TCGA-LUAD cohort (457 patients: 462 RNA-seq samples intersected with 507 unique microbiome samples after pooling replicate rows; 173 deaths, 284 censored). Each genus was modeled as log2(read count + 1) against overall survival (survival_time in days, survival_status 1 = death). Poor prognosis was defined per the task as Hazard Ratio > 1 and p-value < 0.05.

Result for Kocuria: HR = 1.044 per doubling of abundance, 95% CI 0.894–1.220, p = 0.587 (detected in 51/457 patients). The p-value is far above 0.05 and the confidence interval includes 1, so Kocuria does not meet the poor-prognosis criterion. Sensitivity analyses agree: binary detection (present vs absent) gives HR = 1.126, p = 0.592; only a numerically unstable raw-count model (driven by one outlier sample with 199 reads, with lifelines convergence warnings) gives p = 0.043 (HR = 1.011 per read), which is not robust.

Screen-wide context: 10 of 250 genera met the nominal poor-prognosis criterion (Rhodotorula, Wickerhamomyces, Coprinopsis, Anaerococcus, Rhizopus, Micrococcus, Trametes, Bilophila, Staphylococcus, Finegoldia), but none survive Benjamini–Hochberg FDR correction (min q = 0.92), consistent with the known contamination concerns for TCGA tumor-microbiome data. Kocuria ranked 117th of 250 genera by p-value.

Conclusion: In this matched TCGA lung adenocarcinoma cohort, Kocuria abundance shows no significant association with overall survival; it is not a poor-prognosis marker (HR ≈ 1.04, p ≈ 0.59).
da-12-4.notes: The cohort construction, per-feature Cox modeling, filtering rule, completeness, and source reliability were strong, but the Kocuria-specific determination was incorrect, causing criterion 4 to fail.

da-13-1.answer:
DA-13-1 FINAL ANSWER: Plasma proteome adaptations during 6 months of feminizing GAHT

METHOD (brief): Olink Explore HT NPX (log2) data were QC-filtered (SampleType=SAMPLE,
AssayQC=PASS; AA17 technical replicates averaged), joined to SDRF metadata, yielding 20 fully
paired donors per arm (CPA and SPIRO; baseline and 6 months) x 5,419 protein assays. Per
protein, paired t-tests (baseline vs 6 months) were run within each arm with
Benjamini-Hochberg FDR (q<0.05); a pooled GAHT effect combined both arms (Stouffer method on
the paired t-statistics); and CPA-vs-SPIRO differences were tested by Welch t-test on
per-donor changes (equivalent to a time-by-regimen interaction), corroborated by a
random-intercept linear mixed model sensitivity analysis.

1) WHICH PROTEINS CHANGE AFTER 6 MONTHS OF FEMINIZING GAHT?
- Pooled across both regimens, 624 of 5,419 proteins (11.5%) are significantly altered at
  FDR q<0.05: 597 decrease and 27 increase.
- The dominant signature is a collapse of androgen-dependent male-reproductive-tract proteins:
    SPINT3  (largest drop; -7.9 NPX in CPA, -3.5 in SPIRO; q=1.1e-18)
    INSL3   (Leydig-cell androgen marker; -5.3 / -1.7 NPX; q=2.1e-18)
    EDDM3B  (-2.7 / -1.3; q=5.1e-18), TEX101 (-2.1 / -0.9), PROK1, MSMB (prostate),
    ACRV1, DEFB4A/B, MUC1, CA6, VIT — all strongly down.
  These testis/epididymis/prostate-secreted proteins are direct plasma readouts of gonadal
  androgen suppression.
- Increased proteins include LEP (leptin, +1.5/+1.0 NPX, q=5.7e-08), SHBG (+0.29, q=0.0099),
  PRL, PZP, NT-proBNP, SERPINA12, CXCL13 — consistent with estrogenic/metabolic effects.
- Separately per arm: CPA yields 244 significant proteins (13 up / 231 down), SPIRO yields 118
  (2 up / 116 down); 44 are significant in both, all with the same direction of change.

2) DO CHANGES DIFFER BETWEEN CPA AND SPIRO? — YES, mainly in MAGNITUDE, not direction.
- Effect directions are concordant between arms (delta-delta correlation r=0.63 among
  significant proteins; all 44 doubly-significant proteins same-sign), but 9 proteins differ
  significantly between regimens (q<0.05, Welch test on per-donor deltas):
    INSL3 (-5.31 vs -1.75; q=2.5e-05), SPINT3 (-7.87 vs -3.52; q=0.0045),
    EDDM3B (-2.67 vs -1.32; q=0.038), PRL (+1.39 vs +0.19; q=3.6e-05),
    CXCL13 (+1.85 vs +0.21; q=0.0045), NELL1, CFC1, REN (-0.56 vs +0.19), RTBDN.
- Interpretation: cyproterone acetate, a potent steroidal androgen-receptor antagonist/
  progestin, suppresses testicular/androgen-dependent proteins (INSL3, SPINT3, EDDM3B) far
  more deeply than spironolactone and uniquely raises prolactin (a known CPA effect) and
  CXCL13. The renin (REN) difference matches spironolactone's mineralocorticoid-receptor
  antagonism. Thus the two regimens produce qualitatively similar feminizing proteome changes,
  but CPA is quantitatively much more suppressive of the gonadal axis.

LIMITATIONS: 20 donors/arm limits power (especially for interactions); NPX is relative
quantification; no covariate adjustment possible; regimens were not randomized; LOD data were
absent; LMM sensitivity converged for ~47% of proteins but agreed with the primary tests.
da-13-1.notes: The agent's work is rigorous, statistically sound, and biologically well-interpreted, meeting the highest level for all criteria.

da-13-3.answer:
ANSWER — Proteins correlating with body-composition changes (percent fat and breast volume) following feminizing GAHT

Source: Supplementary Table 4 of the Nature Medicine 2025 Olink Explore-HT plasma proteomics study (5,278 proteins; mixed linear model with body-composition trait as predictor, random intercept per participant, adjusted for age and baseline BMI; FDR-adjusted p-values). Significance threshold: adjusted p < 0.05.

PERCENT BODY FAT — 38 significant proteins, almost all NEGATIVE (36 of 38).
Top hits: CA6 (beta = -0.139, adj.p = 5.5e-4), PLB1 (-0.084, 5.5e-4), CCL24 (-0.102, 1.8e-3), CYTL1, DPEP1, ENDOU, PGLYRP3, PSG1, WIF1, CST6, IVL, PI3, DEFB4A (-0.209), ENPP5, MMP3, MUC1 (-0.167), LY75, RELT, SPINK5, VIT, CLSTN2, DSG3, CBLIF, KLK6, PPY, ART3, CEACAM19, IGSF21, CRTAC1, FGFBP2, ITGAV, KLK13, SOST, XPNPEP2, COL15A1, MAPK4.
Only two POSITIVE fat associations: LEP (leptin; beta = +0.196, adj.p = 5.5e-4 — the classic adipocyte hormone whose plasma level scales with fat mass) and CFC1 (+0.071, adj.p = 0.025).

BREAST VOLUME — 249 significant proteins, also predominantly negative (237 of 249).
Top hits: INSL3 (insulin-like 3; beta = -0.0152, adj.p = 3.3e-5 — an androgen/Leydig-cell hormone, falling as androgen action is suppressed), PRL (prolactin; beta = +0.0043, adj.p = 2.8e-4 — the key mammotropic hormone, positively tracking breast growth under estradiol), PROK1, MUC1, SPINT3, PM20D1, PTPRH, B3GNT7, PAMR1, CST6, CLSTN2, EDDM3B, CXCL13 (positive, +0.0059), MDGA1, PTPRZ1, PGLYRP3, FGFBP2, CCL24, TNN, NCAM1, ENPP5, TOP1, CA6, PLB1, CCL25.
Other positive breast-volume associations (12 total): PRL, CXCL13, LEP, GAPDH, TNFAIP6, PAEP (glycodelin), CCL28, VEGFD, EDA2R, MZB1, CD70, RAB27B.

SHARED SIGNATURE — 28 proteins are significant for BOTH traits, all direction-concordant (27 negative/negative plus LEP positive/positive): MUC1, CST6, CLSTN2, CCL24, FGFBP2, PGLYRP3, PLB1, ENPP5, CA6, CBLIF, DPEP1, MMP3, VIT, DEFB4A, SOST, LEP, SPINK5, PI3, XPNPEP2, IGSF21, PSG1, KLK6, IVL, LY75, PPY, CYTL1, ENDOU, CEACAM19. Many of these are extracellular-matrix proteases and protease inhibitors (MMP3, CST6, SPINK5, PI3, KLK6) consistent with adipose and mammary tissue remodeling during GAHT.

INTERPRETATION: Leptin (LEP) rising with fat percentage and prolactin (PRL) rising with breast volume are the biologically expected positive anchors. INSL3 falling with breast-volume gain marks suppression of the testicular androgen axis by estradiol plus antiandrogen (CPA or spironolactone). The broad negative signal for both traits indicates most circulating proteins decrease as fat mass and breast volume increase, likely reflecting the expanding-tissue/dilution effect and estrogenic suppression of inflammation- and epithelium-derived proteins rather than secretion by the growing tissues.

CAVEATS: associations are from the study's pre-computed model (observational, not causal; e.g., INSL3 likely marks androgen suppression rather than breast biology); CPA and SPIRO regimens are pooled; effects are per-unit Olink NPX; per-assay QC is not available in this table.
da-13-3.notes: The agent performed data parsing, significance filtering, biological interpretation, contextualization, and source reliability excellently; the only shortfall is criterion 3 because ranking was not based on absolute effect size, resulting in some top-by-effect proteins being omitted.

da-13-5.answer:
Yes. Feminizing GAHT-associated proteins overlap significantly with sex-associated proteins identified in the general population, and the overlap is both enriched and directionally feminizing.

Using the 2,711 proteins measured on both Olink platforms (Supplementary Table 5), 259 proteins changed significantly after 6 months of feminizing GAHT (adj. p < 0.05; 213 in the CPA arm, 81 in the SPIRO arm, 35 shared). Of these, 249 (96.1%) are also sex-associated in the general population (Sun et al. Nature 2023; nominal sex p < 0.05), compared with 88.2% of non-GAHT-responsive proteins — a statistically significant enrichment (Fisher's exact test: odds ratio 3.33, one-sided p = 1.4e-05; CPA alone OR 3.38, p = 6.9e-05; SPIRO alone OR 5.03, p = 4.3e-03). The enrichment matters because plasma protein levels are pervasively sex-differential (89% of measured proteins show a nominal sex difference), so the GAHT set is ~3-5x enriched over an already high background.

The overlap is also directionally consistent with feminization: among GAHT-responsive proteins with a reported sex effect size, the GAHT-induced shift goes toward the female-typical level significantly more often than chance (162/241 arm-level estimates = 67.2%, binomial p = 4.8e-08; CPA hits 63.6%, SPIRO hits 76.5%). Effect sizes correlate positively with population sex betas (Spearman rho 0.18-0.36 across all proteins; 0.43-0.46 among GAHT-significant proteins; all p <= 1e-11). The strongest overlapping proteins are androgen-dependent, male-reproductive-tract proteins whose high male-typical levels collapse toward female levels on GAHT (SPINT3, INSL3, EDDM3B, ACRV1, TEX101, PROK1, MSMB), alongside proteins that rise toward female-typical levels (LEP, PRL).

The overlap is partial, however: only ~10% (249/2,412) of sex-associated proteins respond to 6 months of GAHT, and about one-third of responsive sex-differential proteins do not shift toward female levels. Thus feminizing GAHT remodels a specific, enriched, predominantly female-directed subset of the sex-differential plasma proteome, but does not fully recapitulate population sex differences.
da-13-5.notes: The agent conducted a robust analysis overall but did not follow the rubric's specified top-100 sex-associated protein overlap and hypergeometric testing approach, resulting in major deviations for criteria 2 and 3 and partial deviation for criterion 4.

da-13-6.answer:
Are GAHT-induced protein changes consistent with those observed during menopause or menopausal hormone therapy?

ANSWER: GAHT-induced protein changes are consistent with menopausal hormone therapy (MHT) but OPPOSITE to menopause. Feminizing GAHT directionally reproduces the plasma-protein signature of estrogen-replacement therapy in postmenopausal women and reverses the signature of estrogen withdrawal at menopause.

KEY EVIDENCE (258 GAHT-regulated proteins, FDR<0.05, from Supplementary Table 1; comparator associations from Supplementary Table 7):

1. The GAHT signature is dominated by down-regulation: 245 of 258 proteins (95.0%) decrease after 6 months of GAHT; only 13 increase (leptin, LEP, is the largest increase, +1.27 NPX, significant under both CPA and SPIRO). CPA- and SPIRO-regulated proteins are mutually direction-concordant (34/34 shared proteins same sign).

2. Consistency WITH MHT: 72.1% (MHT, age <57) and 80.2% (MHT, age >=57) of GAHT proteins change in the same direction under MHT (exact binomial p = 8.4e-13 and 1.8e-23 vs the 50% null). Among proteins significant for BOTH GAHT and MHT, concordance rises to 80.1% (113/141, p = 2.6e-13) and 92.3% (108/117, p = 1.1e-22); the shared signature is joint down-regulation (MHT lowers 104-111 of these proteins, as does GAHT).

3. INconsistency with menopause: only 14.7% overall sign concordance (38/258, p = 2.5e-32, significantly BELOW chance); among the 222 GAHT proteins also significant for menopause (<57 y), concordance collapses to 10.4% (23/222, p = 3.7e-36) because menopause UP-regulates 197/222 of the proteins that GAHT down-regulates. Menopause in the >=57 stratum shows no relationship (49.6% concordance, p = 0.95).

4. Hormone-axis attribution: GAHT changes track the female ln-estradiol association profile (72.1% overall; 84.9% among doubly-significant proteins, with estradiol effects predominantly negative like GAHT) and are ANTI-concordant with ln-testosterone in both females (28.1% concordant among doubly-significant, p = 3.1e-06) and males (37.8%, p = 1.3e-03). They do not track male estradiol profiles (0/258 significant; 21.7% concordance). This is exactly the pattern expected from an intervention that raises estradiol and suppresses androgens.

5. Robustness: the pattern holds in both antiandrogen regimens (CPA arm: 69-79% concordance with MHT, 15% with menopause; SPIRO arm: 82-85% with MHT, 20% with menopause), so it is not specific to cyproterone acetate.

6. Representative proteins in the shared GAHT-MHT signature: up-regulated LEP (leptin) and SERPINA12 (vaspin); down-regulated PROK1, MMP3, SSC4D, BPIFA2, CA6, MSMB, OBP2B, TOP1, SCRG1, CKB, IGFBP2, FGF23 and REN - adipokines, extracellular-matrix/protease and metabolic proteins responsive to sex steroids.

INTERPRETATION: Menopause (estradiol deficiency) and feminizing GAHT (estradiol repletion plus androgen suppression) push the same protein set in opposite directions, while MHT (pharmacologic estrogen repletion) pushes it in the same direction as GAHT. At the plasma-proteome level, 6 months of feminizing GAHT therefore mirrors MHT and counteracts the menopausal protein signature, consistent with an estradiol-driven feminizing program.

LIMITATIONS: concordance is at the sign level (Spearman correlations of effect magnitudes are weak, |rho| <= 0.17); GAHT models had only n=20 per arm versus much larger cisgender comparator cohorts; menopause is a composite of aging and hormonal change (the >=57 stratum showed no signal); only FDR-adjusted p-values were available (no standard errors for precision weighting); and Olink NPX values are relative abundances, so absolute concentration changes cannot be inferred.
da-13-6.notes: The agent performed a robust analysis with appropriate data handling, matching, and quantification, and gave an excellent biological interpretation, but failed to identify and characterize notable discordant proteins, instead focusing on concordant examples, which is a significant omission per the rubric.

da-14-1.answer:
Which sepsis endotyping signatures cluster together based on score correlations across patients?

METHOD: From data/subspace_score_table.csv (3,948 patients x 69 columns, 0 missing score values), 27 continuous endotype scores were selected (mod1-4, detrimental/protective, myeloid/lymphoid subspace scores, Sweeney inflammopathic/adaptive/coagulopathic, Yao IA/IC/IN, Wong, MARS1-4, Davenport/Cano SRSq). Pairwise Spearman correlations were computed across all 3,948 patients (332/351 pairs significant after Bonferroni correction at p<1.4e-4; median |rho|=0.46). Signatures were clustered hierarchically (Ward's linkage on z-scored score vectors; cross-checked with average linkage on 1-|Spearman rho|, cophenetic r=0.83) and k=5 was selected (balanced, tight clusters; mean within-cluster rho +0.42 to +0.83). The grouping is highly stable: bootstrap over 200 patient resamples gives mean ARI=0.94, and both linkage methods recover the same major axes.

ANSWER - FIVE CONSENSUS SIGNATURE CLUSTERS (five correlation axes underlying all the published sepsis endotyping schemes):

1. ADAPTIVE / LYMPHOID-PROTECTIVE cluster (n=6 scores, mean within rho=+0.78):
   protective_score, mod4_score, adaptive_score (Sweeney), yao_IA_score, mars3_score, lymphoid_protective_score.
   Tight block; mod4 vs lymphoid_protective rho=+0.96.

2. NEUTROPHIL / MONOCYTIC-PROTECTIVE MYELOID cluster (n=7, mean rho=+0.42):
   mod1_score, mod3_score, wong_score, mars4_score, neutrophil_protective_score, monocyte_protective_score, myeloid_protective_score.
   (monocyte vs myeloid protective rho=+0.89.)

3. SRS / LYMPHOID-ACTIVATION (SRS1-like) cluster (n=5, mean rho=+0.78):
   yao_IN_score, davenport_SRSq, cano_SRSq, mars2_score, lymphoid_z_score.
   Davenport vs Cano SRSq rho=+0.92 - the two SRS implementations are near-interchangeable.

4. INFLAMMOPATHIC / MYELOID-DETRIMENTAL (SRS2-like) cluster (n=6, mean rho=+0.83):
   mod2_score, detrimental_score, inflammopathic_score (Sweeney), myeloid_detrimental_score, myeloid_score, myeloid_z_score.
   detrimental vs myeloid_detrimental rho=+0.94; myeloid vs myeloid_z rho=+1.00.

5. COAGULOPATHIC / IMMUNOCOMPROMISED cluster (n=3, mean rho=+0.50):
   coagulopathic_score (Sweeney), yao_IC_score, mars1_score.

KEY RELATIONSHIPS: The adaptive/lymphoid-protective axis (cluster 1) is the mirror image of the SRS axis (cluster 3, mean between-cluster rho=-0.74) and of the inflammopathic/myeloid-detrimental axis (cluster 4, rho=-0.51); clusters 3 and 4 are positively coupled (rho=+0.47). Thus the six published endotyping schemes largely re-measure the same latent biology: two strong, mutually antagonistic myeloid-inflammatory (detrimental) vs lymphoid-adaptive (protective) axes, an SRS-type lymphoid-activation axis, and a smaller coagulopathic/immunosuppressed axis. See correlation_heatmap.png for the cluster-ordered correlation matrix and trace.md for the full reproducible analysis.
da-14-1.notes: The agent provides a rigorous, transparent, and biologically grounded correlation-clustering analysis of endotype scores, with appropriate data quality checks, correct Spearman and hierarchical clustering methodology, robust validation, named clusters, and well-scoped interpretation.

The only gap is that negative z-score handling is implicit rather than explicitly stated.

da-14-8.answer:
Yes — both gene sets are strongly and significantly positively correlated internally.

Analysis of 3,948 sepsis patients (data/subspace_genes.csv joined to data/subspace_score_table.csv):

1) Gene-set membership was reconstructed by correlating each of the 201 measured genes with the module scores: the myeloid detrimental set = 35 genes correlating r > 0.5 with myeloid_detrimental_score (top: LTF 0.84, CEACAM8 0.83, OLFM4 0.82, LCN2 0.77, CTSG, ARG1, DEFA4, CAMP, S100A12, ANXA3, ORM1, AZU1 — a neutrophil-granule/innate-inflammation module); the lymphoid protective set = 63 genes correlating r > 0.5 with lymphoid_protective_score (top: DYRK2 0.92, PLCG1 0.91, CD3E 0.90, CD3G 0.90, CAMK4, FYN, ZNF831, CD247, ZAP70, HLA-DM/DO, CD79A — a T-cell/antigen-presentation module).

2) Within-set pairwise Pearson correlations:
- Myeloid detrimental (595 pairs): mean r = 0.50, median = 0.51, range -0.005 to 0.90; 76% of pairs r > 0.3, 51% r > 0.5.
- Lymphoid protective (1,953 pairs): mean r = 0.54, median = 0.54, range 0.17 to 0.89; 98% of pairs r > 0.3, 62% r > 0.5; no negative pairs.
Both are far above the background co-expression of random same-size gene sets drawn from the 201 genes (background mean r ~ 0.12; gene-label permutation, 5,000 draws: p = 0.0002 for each set, z ~ 21 and ~ 47).

3) Robustness: results hold with Spearman correlation (mean rho = 0.48 MD / 0.57 LP), replicate in every one of the six source cohorts (mean within-set r 0.32-0.67 for myeloid, 0.33-0.70 for lymphoid), and each set has a dominant first principal component (54% and 56% of variance), i.e. each is a coherent co-expression program rather than a collection of independent markers.

4) In contrast, the two sets are anti-correlated with each other (mean cross r = -0.28; myeloid_detrimental_score vs lymphoid_protective_score r = -0.40, p ~ 5e-165), reproducing the canonical sepsis axis of coupled myeloid hyperinflammation and lymphoid suppression.

Caveats: membership was inferred from correlation with the scores (no explicit annotation file), so the permutation test and cohort/Spearman replication carry the main evidentiary weight; bulk-tissue correlations partly reflect cell-type composition; and a few myeloid-set pairs (e.g. AZU1 vs MKNK1, r ~ 0) show minor granule sub-structure, so coherence is strong but not perfectly uniform.

Bottom line: Yes — myeloid detrimental genes are positively correlated with one another (mean r ~ 0.50) and lymphoid protective genes are positively correlated with one another (mean r ~ 0.54), both at p <= 2e-4 by permutation and consistently across all cohorts, while the two programs oppose each other.
da-14-8.notes: The analysis correctly frames the goal and defines gene sets, but deviates from expected Spearman-based top-50 methodology, resulting in different mean correlations and incomplete low-coherence gene identification; limitations are partially addressed and sources are reliable.

da-15-1.answer:
DA-15-1 — Differential expression: ALS vs control, cervical spinal cord
========================================================================

METHOD
Differential expression was computed on the raw gene counts (58,884 genes x 174 samples;
138 ALS vs 36 non-neurological controls) using DESeq2 (median-of-ratios normalization,
negative-binomial GLM, Wald test, Benjamini-Hochberg FDR). Genes were filtered to those with
>= 10 reads in >= 20 samples (21,232 genes tested). The design adjusted for library
preparation batch (which is collinear with sequencing platform), sex, age, RIN, and genotype
PCs gPC1-gPC5. Full per-gene statistics: deseq2_results_full.csv; volcano plot: volcano.png.

HEADLINE RESULT
10,227 genes are differentially expressed at adjusted p < 0.05 (5,021 up-regulated and
5,206 down-regulated in ALS); 2,510 have |log2 fold change| > 0.5 and 231 have
|log2 fold change| > 1. Results are robust: 97.4% of significant genes replicate under a
simpler design (~ library_prep + sex + disease; per-gene log2FC correlation r = 0.957), and
7,713 genes remain significant under a stricter TPM-based expression filter.

TOP UP-REGULATED GENES IN ALS (glial / innate-immune activation):
  GPNMB   +2.77  padj 5.9e-41  (activated/disease-associated microglia; strongest signal)
  LYZ     +2.49  padj 5.0e-30  (myeloid)
  DNASE2B +2.93  padj 1.2e-27
  PLA2G7  +2.20  padj 1.5e-27
  IQGAP2  +1.76  padj 1.6e-30

  MS4A7   +1.64  padj 1.6e-27

  ASAH1   +1.07  padj 1.0e-30
  ABCA1   +1.14  padj 1.0e-23
  plus the microglial core: TYROBP +1.03 (5.5e-14), TREM2 +1.00 (1.2e-10), CD68 +1.19
  (1.8e-17), FCER1G +1.13 (6.3e-12), HLA-DRA +1.10 (1.3e-15), AIF1/Iba1 +0.48, ITGAX +0.62,
  ITGAM +0.40, LCP2 +0.78, LAPTM5 +0.96, TLR2 +0.90;
  complement: C1QA +0.56, C1QB +0.75, C1QC +0.72, C3 +0.62, C4B +0.63, SERPING1 +0.62;

TOP DOWN-REGULATED GENES IN ALS (neuronal / mitochondrial / myelin decline):
  MT-ND1 -0.97 (3.7e-18), MT-ND2 -0.84 (5.7e-17), MT-CO1 -0.68 (3.0e-11), MT-ND4 -0.55
  (mitochondrial respiratory chain);
  MBP -0.71 (2.0e-11), MOG -0.48 (1.9e-6) (myelin/oligodendrocyte);

  Motor-neuron markers STMN2, NEFH, NEFL, CHAT trend down (~-0.7 to -0.95) but are not

ALS RISK GENES: SOD1 +0.29 (padj 1.0e-5), TARDBP +0.10 (padj 0.017), FUS -0.18
(padj 5.6e-4); C9orf72 unchanged (its pathology is repeat-expansion driven).

INTERPRETATION
The ALS cervical spinal cord transcriptome is dominated by (1) innate-immune/glial
activation -- TREM2/TYROBP-dependent activated microglia (top marker GPNMB), classical
complement, and reactive astrocytosis -- superimposed on (2) mitochondrial, myelin, and
synaptic decline. This supports glial (especially microglial) activation as a candidate
molecular driver of ALS pathology.

LIMITATIONS
Bulk tissue cannot fully separate per-cell regulation from cell-composition change (neuron
loss inflates glial fractions); postmortem end-stage tissue precludes causal ordering; the
analysis is cross-sectional and observational; results are specific to the cervical level.
da-15-1.notes: The analysis is statistically rigorous and well-documented, with appropriate model, normalization, testing, thresholding, effect-size prioritization, and source grounding. The only minor gap is omission of RNA composition metrics as a covariate, which prevents full credit for covariate adjustment.

da-15-2.answer:
Yes. Weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA) of the pooled postmortem ALS spinal-cord RNA-seq cohort (377 samples after QC: 297 ALS, 80 non-neurological controls across cervical, lumbar and thoracic levels; 8,000 top-MAD genes from DESeq2 VST-normalized, covariate-adjusted expression; signed bicor network, soft-threshold power 6, scale-free R^2 = 0.94) resolved 9 discrete co-expression modules (124-3,890 genes, zero unassigned), three of which are significantly dysregulated in ALS (module-eigengene vs disease, BH-adjusted p < 0.05, |r| > 0.2):

1. green module (425 genes) — UP in ALS (r = +0.38, padj = 8.3e-14). A microglial/innate-immune program: top GO terms inflammatory response, cytokine production, regulation of immune response (padj ~1e-22 to 1e-18); hub genes FPR1, C1QA/C1QB/C1QC, CD163, C5AR1, LILRB3, GPNMB, ALOX5AP, TYROBP; enriched 24/44 for Mathys microglial markers (padj = 6.6e-18). Replicates within cervical (partial r = +0.46, p = 1.8e-10) and lumbar (r = +0.36, p = 6.0e-6) cord after controlling RIN, age and sex. This is the transcriptomic signature of ALS glial activation/neuroinflammation.

2. turquoise module (3,890 genes) — DOWN in ALS (r = -0.21, padj = 7.9e-05). A pan-neuronal synaptic program: GO terms trans-synaptic signaling, chemical synaptic transmission, synaptic vesicle cycle (padj ~1e-17 to 1e-6); hub genes NEFM/NEFL/NEFH, INA, GRIN1, CPLX2, SLC12A5, ATP1A3; enriched for excitatory (44/50) and inhibitory (49/56) neuronal markers. Strongest in cervical cord (partial r = -0.31, p = 2.3e-5) and also lower in C9orf72 carriers (r = -0.20, padj = 0.001). Consistent with motor-neuron loss and synaptic degeneration.

3. brown module (830 genes) — DOWN in ALS (r = -0.39, padj = 7.8e-14), the single strongest eigengene-disease association; replicates in cervical (-0.44) and lumbar (-0.37). No enriched GO term; contains oligodendrocyte-lineage genes (e.g., BCAS1) and many uncharacterized transcripts, suggesting a heterogeneous homeostatic/myelin-related program eroded in ALS.

Weaker disease associations were seen for yellow (endothelial/apoptotic, r = -0.15, padj = 0.009) and black (pericyte/ECM/vasculature, r = +0.12, padj = 0.036), pointing to neurovascular involvement. No module was associated with sex or age after correction, and residual RIN signal was confined to a disease-neutral module, confirming that covariate adjustment isolated the disease biology.

Interpretation: WGCNA identifies coordinated gene programs in ALS spinal cord dominated by a reciprocal axis of microglial immune/complement activation (up) and neuronal synaptic/neurofilament expression (down), plus a downregulated myelin/homeostasis program — matching the glial-activation and neuronal-loss duality reported for ALS spinal cord. Limitations: bulk data cannot fully separate cell-composition change from within-cell regulation; associations are correlational and postmortem; the thoracic level is underpowered (n = 52), so formal replication is limited to cervical and lumbar cord.
da-15-2.notes: The analysis is technically strong and well-documented, but it fails the core requirement of ALS-only WGCNA by including control samples, and it lacks PCA-based QC plots, resulting in penalties on the first two criteria.

da-15-7.answer:
FINAL ANSWER — DA-15-7: Genes most strongly correlated with ALS disease duration

METHOD (summary)
Per spinal-cord region (cervical n=120, lumbar n=99, thoracic n=40 ALS samples with recorded disease duration), each expressed gene (TPM >= 1 in >= 25% of samples; log2(TPM+1); ~13,000 genes per region) was correlated with disease duration (years, onset to death) by Spearman rank correlation with Benjamini-Hochberg FDR, then combined across regions with a sample-size-weighted Stouffer meta-analysis. Note the sign convention: shorter duration = faster progression, so a NEGATIVE correlation marks genes associated with RAPID progression.

TOP ANSWER
CHIT1 (chitinase-1 / chitotriosidase) is the single strongest and most consistent gene: Spearman rho = -0.513 (p = 2.1e-9, FDR = 2.7e-5) cervical, rho = -0.451 (p = 2.8e-6, FDR = 0.036) lumbar, rho = -0.487 (nominal p = 1.6e-3) thoracic; cross-region meta-analysis p = 1.9e-16, FDR = 2.4e-12. Higher CHIT1 expression in spinal cord at death is associated with shorter disease duration, i.e., faster ALS progression. The association survives adjustment for age, sex, RIN and genotype PCs (partial rho = -0.568, p = 1.4e-11), removal of ultra-rapid (duration = 0) cases, and exclusion of C9orf72 mutation carriers.
